Abingdon
AB-ing-dun
n. (the Berkshire town whose great abbey was dissolved in 1538 and whose townsmen then rebuilt its civic and charitable life for themselves)
Old English Abbandun, Abba's hill; the monastery took its name from the hill and gave it to the town.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Abingdon is the Thames-side town below Oxford, and until 1538 it was essentially the property of its abbey. The Benedictine house, refounded in the tenth century, was one of the richest in England, holding the manor, the market, the mills and the bridge tolls, and the townsmen had rioted against it more than once over their want of a parish church of their own and over the abbot's control of trade. At the Dissolution the house was surrendered and almost entirely demolished for its stone, so that very little of it now stands. What followed is the part the dictionary records. The town obtained a charter in 1556, became the county town of Berkshire, refounded its school as Roysse's in 1563 out of a merchant's bequest, maintained Christ's Hospital with its almshouses from an older guild endowment, and built the county hall in the sixteen-seventies. Its dissenting congregations, Baptist and Presbyterian, were vigorous from the Restoration onward. The dictionary records Abingdon as a case of a town taking up, for itself and badly at first, the schooling and the relief of the poor that an abbey had done for it, and holds that this was the right direction of travel.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines an almshouse as a house for the poor; a charter as a written instrument of privileges; a breach as a gap; to repair as to restore; and reproach as censure or shame.

expand to see more

ALMSHOUSE, n. A house appropriated for the use of the poor; a house maintained by charity.

CHARTER, n. A written instrument, executed with usual forms, given as evidence of a grant or privilege.

BREACH, n. The act of breaking; a gap or opening made by breaking; the violation of a law or covenant.

REPAIR, v.t. To restore to a sound or good state after decay, waste or injury; to mend; to rebuild.

REPROACH, n. Censure mingled with contempt; scorn; the cause of shame or disgrace.

Key Scripture

Neh 1:3 — "And they said unto me, The remnant that are left of the captivity there in the province are in great affliction and reproach: the wall of Jerusalem also is broken down, and the gates thereof are burned with fire."

Neh 2:17 — "Then said I unto them, Ye see the distress that we are in, how Jerusalem lieth waste, and the gates thereof are burned with fire: come, and let us build up the wall of Jerusalem, that we be no more a reproach."

Neh 6:3 — "And I sent messengers unto them, saying, I am doing a great work, so that I cannot come down: why should the work cease, whilst I leave it, and come down to you?"

Dan 9:19 — "O Lord, hear; O Lord, forgive; O Lord, hearken and do; defer not, for thine own sake, O my God: for thy city and thy people are called by thy name."

Modern Corruption

Thames-side Berkshire town owned by its Benedictine abbey until 1538, demolished for its stone, after which the townsmen obtained a charter, refounded their school and maintained their own almshouses.

expand to see more

The corruption to name is the monastic lordship of a town, and the dictionary names it as the real grievance the Abingdon rioters had long before any reformer reached them. The abbey held the market, the mills, the bridge tolls and the right of presentation, and would not let the townsmen have a parish church they could call theirs; relief of the poor and schooling came as the abbot's charity rather than as the town's duty. A religious house that owns a town does both of them harm. When it went, the townsmen were left with Nehemiah's situation and had to make Nehemiah's answer: the report was that “the wall of Jerusalem also is broken down, and the gates thereof are burned with fire” (Neh 1:3), and the response was not a lament but a proposal, “come, and let us build up the wall of Jerusalem, that we be no more a reproach” (Neh 2:17).

The second paragraph names what the dictionary thinks the right direction of travel was, and it is not nostalgia for the abbey. A charter in 1556, a school refounded out of a merchant's bequest in 1563, almshouses kept out of a guild endowment, a county hall in the sixteen-seventies and strong Baptist and Presbyterian congregations by the end of the century: that is a town doing for itself, under God, what had been done for it. The work is slow and gets interrupted, and the proper reply to those who would call a man down from it is Nehemiah's: “I am doing a great work, so that I cannot come down” (Neh 6:3). The dictionary adds the prayer that belongs with such rebuilding, which is a prayer about God's name and not the town's credit: “O Lord, hear; O Lord, forgive; O Lord, hearken and do; defer not, for thine own sake, O my God” (Dan 9:19). An abbey reduced to a gateway and a town that learned to keep its own poor is, on balance, a gain.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew chomah (H2346), a wall; Hebrew cherpah (H2781), reproach; Hebrew banah (H1129), to build.

expand to see more

Hebrew chomah (H2346) — a wall, a rampart; “the wall of Jerusalem also is broken down”, Nehemiah 1:3.

Hebrew cherpah (H2781) — reproach, shame, disgrace; “that we be no more a reproach”, Nehemiah 2:17.

Hebrew banah (H1129) — to build, to rebuild, to establish; “let us build up the wall of Jerusalem”, Nehemiah 2:17.

Hebrew mela'kah (H4399) — work, business, occupation; “I am doing a great work, so that I cannot come down”, Nehemiah 6:3.

Hebrew 'achar (H309) — to delay, to tarry, to defer; “defer not, for thine own sake, O my God”, Daniel 9:19.

Usage

"“the gates thereof are burned with fire” (Neh 1:3) — the abbey demolished for its stone, 1538."

"“let us build up the wall of Jerusalem” (Neh 2:17) — a charter in 1556 and a school in 1563."

"“I am doing a great work, so that I cannot come down” (Neh 6:3) — a town keeping its own poor."
